topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, a power-driven vessel less than 12 meters in length must have sidelights visible for a minimum distance of:
choice_a: 1 mile
choice_b: 2 miles
choice_d: 5 miles
explanation: For vessels less than 12 meters in length, sidelights must be visible for at least 1 mile under the Inland Navigation Rules' light visibility requirements.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22, Inland Navigation Rules - Visibility of Lights (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, a power-driven vessel less than 12 meters in length must have a masthead (steaming) light visible for a minimum distance of:
choice_a: 1 mile
choice_b: 2 miles
choice_d: 5 miles
explanation: For vessels less than 12 meters, the masthead light must be visible for at least 2 miles.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22, Inland Navigation Rules - Visibility of Lights (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: For both vessels less than 12 meters and vessels 12 to 50 meters in length, the sternlight must be visible for a minimum distance of:
choice_a: 1 mile
choice_b: 3 miles
choice_d: 6 miles
explanation: The sternlight visibility requirement is 2 miles for both vessels under 12 meters and vessels 12 to 50 meters; only vessels 50 meters or more require 3 miles of visibility.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22, Inland Navigation Rules - Visibility of Lights (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A power-driven vessel 12 meters or more but less than 20 meters in length must have a masthead light visible for at least:
choice_a: 2 miles
choice_b: 5 miles
choice_d: 3 miles
explanation: Vessels 12 to 50 meters in length require a masthead light visible 5 miles, except that vessels under 20 meters only need 3 miles.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22, Inland Navigation Rules - Visibility of Lights (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A power-driven vessel 20 meters or more but less than 50 meters in length must have a masthead light visible for at least:
choice_a: 5 miles
choice_b: 3 miles
choice_d: 6 miles
explanation: Vessels 20 to 50 meters in length require a masthead light visible at least 5 miles.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22, Inland Navigation Rules - Visibility of Lights (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel 50 meters or more in length must have a masthead light visible for at least:
choice_a: 5 miles
choice_b: 6 miles
choice_d: 2 miles
explanation: Vessels 50 meters or more in length require a masthead light visible at least 6 miles, the longest range of any vessel size category.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22, Inland Navigation Rules - Visibility of Lights (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, a power-driven vessel underway must normally exhibit which combination of lights?
choice_a: Only a masthead light and an anchor light
choice_b: Sidelights and a sternlight only, with no masthead light
choice_c: A masthead light forward, sidelights, and a sternlight
choice_d: An all-round red light and a sternlight only
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway must show a masthead light forward, sidelights, and a sternlight; a second masthead light abaft and higher than the forward one is optional for vessels under 50 meters.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.23, Inland Navigation Rules - Power-Driven Vessels Underway (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A power-driven vessel less than 12 meters in length may, instead of the standard masthead-and-sternlight arrangement, exhibit which lights?
choice_a: A single all-round red light only
choice_b: Two all-round white lights and no sidelights
choice_d: An all-round white light and sidelights
explanation: Vessels under 12 meters may, in lieu of the standard configuration, exhibit an all-round white light together with sidelights.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.23, Inland Navigation Rules - Power-Driven Vessels Underway (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: At night, what is the key difference between the running lights of a sailing vessel under sail alone and a power-driven vessel underway?
choice_a: A sailing vessel shows sidelights and a sternlight but no masthead light
choice_b: A sailing vessel shows a masthead light but no sidelights
choice_c: A sailing vessel shows only a sternlight
choice_d: There is no difference; both show identical lights
explanation: A sailing vessel underway displays sidelights and a sternlight but, unlike a power-driven vessel, no masthead light -- the absence of a masthead light is how a sailing vessel is distinguished from a powerboat at night.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25, Inland Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessels Underway (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A sailing vessel less than 20 meters in length may combine its sidelights and sternlight into what single arrangement?
choice_a: A single all-round red light at the bow
choice_b: One tri-color lantern carried at or near the top of the mast
choice_c: Two masthead lights in a vertical line
choice_d: A flashing yellow light at the stern
explanation: Sailing vessels under 20 meters may combine the sidelights and sternlight into one tri-color lantern carried at or near the top of the mast where it can best be seen.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25, Inland Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessels Underway (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A sailing vessel may optionally exhibit which additional lights at or near the top of the mast, provided they are not combined with a tri-color lantern?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, green over red
choice_b: A single flashing white light
choice_c: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over green
choice_d: A red sidelight only
explanation: A sailing vessel may optionally exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line at or near the top of the mast, with the upper light red and the lower light green, but not in combination with the tri-color lantern option.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25, Inland Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessels Underway (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A sailing vessel less than 7 meters in length, or a vessel under oars, that cannot practicably show the standard sailing lights must at least:
choice_a: Operate only during daylight hours
choice_b: Display a black conical shape at the bow
choice_c: Sound a bell continuously while underway
choice_d: Have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, exhibited in time to prevent collision
explanation: Sailing vessels under 7 meters and vessels under oars must show the standard lights if practicable, or at minimum have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, exhibited in sufficient time to prevent collision.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25, Inland Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessels and Vessels Under Oars (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A sailing vessel that is also being propelled by its engine (a motorsailer) is legally considered a power-driven vessel and, if 12 meters or more in length, must display which additional daytime shape forward?
choice_a: A black conical shape, apex downward
choice_b: A black ball
choice_d: A diamond shape
explanation: A vessel proceeding under sail while also being propelled by machinery is a power-driven vessel and must exhibit forward a black conical shape, apex downward; vessels less than 12 meters are exempt from this shape requirement.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25, Inland Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessels Under Sail and Power (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel at anchor must generally exhibit an all-round white light forward and a second, lower all-round white light in which location?
choice_a: Amidships
choice_b: Near the stern
choice_d: On the port side only
explanation: A vessel at anchor exhibits an all-round white light (or a ball shape) forward, and a second all-round white light at or near the stern, at a lower level than the forward light.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30, Inland Navigation Rules - Anchored Vessels (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel less than 50 meters in length at anchor may simplify the standard two-light anchor arrangement by instead exhibiting:
choice_a: A single red light at the bow
choice_b: Two red lights in a vertical line
choice_c: A single all-round white light where it can best be seen
choice_d: No light is ever required
explanation: Vessels under 50 meters at anchor may exhibit a single all-round white light where it can best be seen, instead of the separate forward and stern anchor lights.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30, Inland Navigation Rules - Anchored Vessels (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel less than 7 meters in length at anchor outside a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or an area where other vessels normally navigate:
choice_a: Must still show both anchor lights at all times
choice_b: Must sound a bell every 2 minutes instead
choice_c: May never anchor outside a marked anchorage
choice_d: Is not required to exhibit anchor lights or shapes
explanation: Vessels under 7 meters are not required to exhibit anchor lights or shapes when anchored outside a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or where other vessels normally navigate.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30, Inland Navigation Rules - Anchored Vessels (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel less than 20 meters in length anchored within a special anchorage area designated by the Coast Guard:
choice_a: Is not required to exhibit anchor lights or shapes
choice_b: Must exhibit two additional white lights
choice_c: Must display a black ball shape at all times
choice_d: Must sound one prolonged blast every 2 minutes
explanation: A vessel under 20 meters at anchor in a special anchorage area designated by the Coast Guard is not required to exhibit the anchor lights and shapes otherwise required.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30, Inland Navigation Rules - Anchored Vessels (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, a vessel 12 meters or more but less than 20 meters in length must be equipped with which sound-signaling device?
choice_a: A whistle and a bell
choice_b: A whistle
choice_d: No sound-signaling device is required
explanation: A vessel of 12 meters or more but less than 20 meters in length need only be provided with a whistle; the bell requirement applies to vessels 20 meters or more.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33, Inland Navigation Rules - Sound Signal Equipment (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel 20 meters or more in length must carry which sound-signaling devices?
choice_a: A whistle only
choice_b: A bell only
choice_d: A gong only
explanation: Vessels 20 meters or more in length must be provided with both a whistle and a bell.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33, Inland Navigation Rules - Sound Signal Equipment (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel 100 meters or more in length must carry a whistle and a bell, and additionally:
choice_a: A second whistle
choice_b: A foghorn powered by compressed air only
choice_d: A gong with a tone that cannot be confused with the bell
explanation: Vessels 100 meters or more in length must also carry a gong whose tone and sound cannot be confused with that of the required bell.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33, Inland Navigation Rules - Sound Signal Equipment (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A vessel less than 12 meters in length is not obligated to carry a whistle and bell, but must:
choice_a: Be provided with some other means of making an efficient sound signal
choice_b: Carry no sound-producing device at all
choice_c: Rely solely on a marine VHF radio
choice_d: Carry a bell only, no whistle
explanation: Vessels less than 12 meters are not required to carry the standard whistle and bell, but must still be provided with some other means of making an efficient sound signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33, Inland Navigation Rules - Sound Signal Equipment (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Per the Virginia Boater's Guide, a boat's sound-producing device -- required even on paddlecraft -- should be capable of producing a signal audible for approximately what minimum distance?
choice_a: 5 nautical miles
choice_b: 1/2 nautical mile
choice_d: 3 nautical miles
explanation: The Virginia Boater's Guide states that a vessel's sound-producing device, required equipment even for paddlecraft, should produce a signal audible for about 1/2 a nautical mile.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Required Equipment (Sound-Producing Devices)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In sight of one another (not in restricted visibility), under the Inland Rules, one short blast of a power-driven vessel's whistle signals what intended maneuver?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_b: I am operating astern propulsion
choice_c: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_d: I am in danger and require assistance
explanation: Under the Inland Rules' maneuvering and warning signals, one short blast means 'I intend to leave you on my port side.'
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(a), Inland Navigation Rules - Maneuvering and Warning Signals (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In sight of one another, two short blasts of a power-driven vessel's whistle signal:
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_b: I am overtaking you on your port side
choice_c: I am altering course to avoid a shoal
choice_d: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
explanation: Under the Inland Rules' maneuvering and warning signals, two short blasts mean 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side.'
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(a), Inland Navigation Rules - Maneuvering and Warning Signals (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Three short blasts of a whistle, given by a vessel in sight of another vessel, indicate:
choice_a: I am operating astern propulsion
choice_b: I am anchoring
choice_d: I intend to overtake on your port side
explanation: Three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion.'
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(a), Inland Navigation Rules - Maneuvering and Warning Signals (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: If a vessel is uncertain about the intentions of another vessel it can see, or doubts that the other vessel is taking sufficient action to avoid collision, it should sound:
choice_a: One prolonged blast
choice_b: At least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle
choice_d: A single short blast
explanation: The danger, or doubt, signal is at least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle, which may be supplemented by a light signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(d), Inland Navigation Rules - Maneuvering and Warning Signals (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: When approaching a bend or an area of a channel where other vessels may be hidden from view, a vessel should sound:
choice_a: Five short blasts
choice_b: Three short blasts
choice_d: Two prolonged blasts
explanation: A vessel nearing a bend or an obscured area of a channel where other vessels may be hidden sounds one prolonged blast, known as the bend signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(e), Inland Navigation Rules - Maneuvering and Warning Signals (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: If a vessel around a blind bend hears another vessel's bend signal, what should it do?
choice_a: Remain silent and proceed as normal
choice_b: Sound the danger signal
choice_d: Answer with a similar prolonged blast
explanation: Any vessel that hears the one prolonged bend signal of a vessel approaching from the other side of the bend must answer with a similar prolonged blast.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(e), Inland Navigation Rules - Maneuvering and Warning Signals (Cornell LII)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Virginia law requires that navigation lights be exhibited on a boat during which times?
choice_a: Between sunset and sunrise, and during periods of restricted visibility
choice_b: Only during periods of restricted visibility
choice_c: Only between sunset and sunrise, never in daytime fog
choice_d: Only when operating on the Chesapeake Bay
explanation: No person may operate a boat without exhibiting the required navigation lights between sunset and sunrise, and lights are also required during periods of restricted visibility.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Required Equipment / Safe Boating (Navigation Lights)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In the U.S. Aids to Navigation System, non-lateral regulatory markers are generally colored:
choice_a: Solid black with white numbers
choice_b: White with orange markings and black lettering
choice_d: Blue with white lettering
explanation: Non-lateral regulatory markers are white and use orange markings with black lettering.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A diamond-shaped symbol on a white regulatory marker warns boaters of:
choice_a: A controlled speed zone
choice_b: Available food, fuel, and repairs
choice_c: A danger such as rocks, shoals, dams, or stumps
choice_d: An area completely closed to boats
explanation: A diamond on a regulatory marker warns of dangers such as rocks, shoals, construction, dams, or stumps, and boaters should proceed with caution and keep a safe distance.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A diamond shape with a cross inside it on a regulatory marker indicates:
choice_a: A place to obtain information or supplies
choice_b: A no-wake or idle-speed zone
choice_c: A safe water channel that may be passed on either side
choice_d: An area off-limits to all boats, such as a swimming area, dam, or spillway
explanation: A crossed diamond marks an area off-limits to all boats, such as a swimming area, dam, or spillway.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A circle on a white regulatory marker indicates:
choice_a: A controlled area, such as no-wake, idle-speed, a speed limit, or a ski zone
choice_b: A danger area to avoid entirely
choice_d: A safe water marker
explanation: A circle on a regulatory marker indicates a controlled area such as no-wake, idle-speed, a speed limit, or a ski zone.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A square on a white regulatory marker is used to provide:
choice_a: A warning of an underwater obstruction
choice_b: Information such as food, supplies, repairs, directions, or distances
choice_c: The boundary of an exclusion zone
choice_d: The location of a designated anchorage only
explanation: A square on a regulatory marker provides non-regulatory information such as places to find food, supplies, and repairs, as well as directions and distances.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Which statement correctly describes a safe water marker (white with red vertical stripes)?
choice_a: It must always be kept to the boat's starboard side
choice_b: It marks a swimming area closed to boats
choice_c: It may be passed on either side because it marks unobstructed water
choice_d: It indicates a speed-controlled zone
explanation: A safe water marker is white with red vertical stripes and indicates unobstructed water on all sides, so it may be passed on either side, unlike lateral channel buoys which must be kept to a specific side.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Other Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A mooring buoy in the U.S. Aids to Navigation System is colored:
choice_a: Solid orange
choice_b: Red and green striped
choice_d: White with a blue horizontal band
explanation: Mooring buoys are white with a blue horizontal band and are typically placed in marinas and anchoring areas.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Other Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Which of the following is true regarding mooring buoys?
choice_a: They are the only buoys a boater may legally tie up to
choice_b: Any navigational buoy may be used for mooring in an emergency
choice_d: They are always unlit and unmarked
explanation: Mooring buoys, marked white with a blue horizontal band, are the only buoys a boater may legally tie up to.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Other Non-Lateral Markers)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: An inland waters obstruction marker, showing white with black vertical stripes, indicates that a boater should:
choice_a: Pass only on the buoy's northern side
choice_b: Not pass between the buoy and the nearest shore
choice_c: Treat it the same as a mid-channel marker
choice_d: Ignore it unless operating at night
explanation: A white buoy with black vertical stripes marks an obstruction to navigation; boaters should not pass between the buoy and the nearest shore.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide / Boat-Ed Virginia Course - Aids to Navigation (Other Non-Lateral Markers)
